<reason>A controlled the meta-frame from Rebuttal 1 onward: catching B's twin concessions ("restoration is a public good," "no permanent veto"), A relentlessly pressed that B's "delay or redesign" test was a slow-motion veto with no certifier or endpoint. When A's Q1 demanded a single reintroduction that could pass B's test despite organized opposition, B conceded Yellowstone—crossing the motion's central hurdle (overriding objection) within B's own framework. A's closing cleanly converted this: every safeguard B demanded already lives inside reintroduction done properly, leaving only "predators on the ground vs meetings." A's rent-vs-own cost comparison and the "compensation is revisable; a lost forest generation is not" asymmetry gave the cleaner decision rule. B's necessity-vs-feasibility distinction was genuinely strong and never fully closed, and B pressed the missing comparative justification well—but after conceding the paradigm case, B was left defending a threshold A had already absorbed, shrinking CON ground far below the motion as written. Both sides were disciplined: proper Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure, plausible background knowledge, no fake sourcing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Pressure Q1 ("who certifies your conditions; name one reintroduction that passes despite organized rural opposition") forced B's Yellowstone concession in B4.1, which A's closing converted into "that is our plan"—the decisive collapse of the override question. B's best counter (agency is a decision-maker, not a justification; potential ≠ presumption) came too late to rebuild a distinct CON route.</best_rebuttal>
